content.title: Suspected pulmonary embolism without haemodynamic instability (sections 7.1.2, 7.1.2.1, 7.1.2.2)
content.summary: Guidance on diagnostic strategies for suspected pulmonary embolism (PE) in haemodynamically stable patients, focusing on use of D-dimer, computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA), and ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy.

sections.heading: Strategy based on computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA)
key_points: In emergency department patients, measurement of plasma D-dimer is the logical first step after assessing clinical probability; it allows PE to be ruled out in a substantial proportion of outpatients.
D-dimer should not be measured in patients with a high clinical probability of PE because of low negative predictive value in that population.
D-dimer is less useful in hospitalized patients because a large number would need testing to obtain a clinically relevant negative result.
In most centers, multidetector CTPA is the second-line test for patients with an elevated D-dimer and the first-line test for patients with a high clinical probability of PE.
CTPA is considered diagnostic of PE when it shows a clot at least at the segmental level of the pulmonary arterial tree.
False-negative CTPA results have been reported in patients with a high clinical probability of PE, but such discrepancies are infrequent and the 3-month thromboembolic risk in these patients was low.

sections.heading: Strategy based on ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy
key_points: Where V/Q scintigraphy is readily available it is a valid option for patients with an elevated D-dimer and a contraindication to CTPA.
V/Q may be preferred over CTPA to avoid radiation, particularly in younger patients and in female patients where thoracic CT might increase lifetime breast cancer risk.
V/Q lung scintigraphy is diagnostic (either normal- or high-probability findings) in a notable proportion of emergency ward patients with suspected PE.
The proportion of diagnostic V/Q scans is higher in patients with a normal chest X-ray; this may support V/Q as a first-line imaging test for PE in younger patients depending on local availability.
Accounting for clinical probability reduces the number of patients with inconclusive V/Q findings.

Patients with a non-diagnostic lung scan and low clinical probability of PE have a low prevalence of confirmed PE; the negative predictive value of this combination is further increased by absence of DVT on lower-limb compression ultrasonography (CUS).

sections.heading: Additional imaging/diagnostic notes
points: Ancillary bedside imaging tests include transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE) which may allow direct visualization of thrombi in the pulmonary artery and its main branches, especially in patients with right ventricular (RV) dysfunction; TOE should be used cautiously in hypoxaemic patients.
Bedside compression ultrasonography (CUS) can detect proximal deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

For unstable patients admitted directly to catheterization laboratory with suspected acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary angiography may be considered after exclusion of acute coronary syndrome, especially if percutaneous catheter-directed treatment is a therapeutic option.
Final confirmation of diagnosis by CT angiography should be sought as soon as the patient is stabilized using supportive treatment.

recommended_clinical_workflow: If low or intermediate probability: measure plasma D-dimer; if negative, PE can be ruled out in many outpatients.

If D-dimer elevated or high clinical probability: proceed to imaging — CTPA is preferred in many centers; V/Q scintigraphy is an alternative where available or when CTPA is contraindicated or to reduce radiation exposure in younger/female patients.
Use clinical probability + imaging results (and lower-limb CUS when indicated) to determine need for further testing or treatment.
